items.title: 4.2 Relationship between mole, molar mass and Avogadro's number

source_refs.note: Topic 4.2, printed pages 76-78, as printed: Sample Problems 4.4 to 4.6, Quick Check 4.2 and both Interesting Information boxes.

blocks.text: A sample of 12.0 grams of natural carbon contains the same number of atoms as 4.0 grams of natural helium. Both samples contain 1 mole of atoms i.e., 6.02 x 10²³.
It is interesting to know that different masses of elements have the same number of atoms.

blocks.latex: \begin{aligned}1.0\ \text{g of hydrogen} &= 1\ \text{mol of hydrogen} = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \text{atoms of H}\\ 23.0\ \text{g of sodium} &= 1\ \text{mol of Na} = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \text{atoms of Na}\\ 238.0\ \text{g of uranium} &= 1\ \text{mol of U} = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \text{atoms of U}\end{aligned}
blocks.text_alt: 1.0 g of hydrogen = 1 mol of hydrogen = 6.02 x 10²³ atoms of H; 23.0 g of sodium = 1 mol of Na = 6.02 x 10²³ atoms of Na; 238.0 g of uranium = 1 mol of U = 6.02 x 10²³ atoms of U

blocks.text: An atom of sodium is 23 times heavier than an atom of hydrogen. In order to have equal number of atoms, sodium should be taken 23 times greater in mass than hydrogen.

blocks.latex: \begin{aligned}18.0\ \text{g of }\ce{H2O} &= 1\ \text{mol of water} = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \text{molecules of water}\\ 180.0\ \text{g of glucose} &= 1\ \text{mol of glucose} = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \text{molecules of glucose}\end{aligned}
blocks.text_alt: 18.0 g of H₂O = 1 mol of water = 6.02 x 10²³ molecules of water; 180.0 g of glucose = 1 mol of glucose = 6.02 x 10²³ molecules of glucose

blocks.text: Hence, one mole of different compounds has different masses but the same number of molecules.
Similarly, the number of ions in one mole of different ionic species is always the same, i.e Avogadro’s number.

blocks.latex: \begin{aligned}96.1\ \text{g of }\ce{SO4^2-} &= 1\ \text{mole of }\ce{SO4^2-} = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \text{ions of }\ce{SO4^2-}\\ 62.0\ \text{g of }\ce{NO3^{1-}} &= 1\ \text{mole of }\ce{NO3^{1-}} = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \text{ions of }\ce{NO3^{1-}}\end{aligned}
blocks.text_alt: 96.1 g of SO₄²⁻ = 1 mole of SO₄²⁻ = 6.02 x 10²³ ions of SO₄²⁻; 62.0 g of NO₃¹⁻ = 1 mole of NO₃¹⁻ = 6.02 x 10²³ ions of NO₃¹⁻

blocks.text: One can calculate the number of moles by dividing the number of particles by Avogadro’s number.

blocks.latex: \text{Number of moles} = \frac{\text{No. of particles of a substance}}{\text{Avogadro's Number}}
blocks.text_alt: Number of moles = No. of particles of a substance / Avogadro’s Number

blocks.text: The relationship between amounts of substances in terms of their moles and the number of particles (atoms, molecules, ions, electrons or particles) is given below:

blocks.latex: \text{Number of particles} = \frac{\text{Mass of subtance} \times N_A}{\text{Molar Mass}}
blocks.text_alt: Number of particles = Mass of subtance x Nₐ / Molar Mass

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The word is printed “subtance”; it is substance: Number of particles = Mass of substance x Nₐ / Molar Mass.

blocks.alt: Three dark blue boxes in a row: 'Mass in grams' on the left, 'Moles' in the middle and 'No. of Particles' on the right. A grey arrow points from Moles to Mass in grams, labelled 'x Molar mass'. A second grey arrow points from Moles to No. of Particles, labelled 'x Avogadro's number'.
blocks.caption: Mass in grams, moles and number of particles (original drawing after the scheme printed on p77 of the textbook).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The left label of the printed scheme reads “Molar x mass”; it is “x Molar mass” (moles x molar mass = mass in grams), as drawn above.

blocks.title: Sample Problem 4.4
blocks.problem: A sample of glucose, contains 3.76 x 10²⁴ molecules of glucose. What is the number of moles in this quantity?
steps: No. of moles of glucose = 3.76 x 10²⁴ molecules / 6.02 x 10²³ molecules mol⁻¹

blocks.title: Sample Problem 4.5
blocks.problem: How many atoms are there in a sodium metal that contains 2.3 g?
steps: Number of moles of sodium = 2.3/23.0 = 0.1 mol
Number of atoms of sodium = Number of moles of sodium x Nₐ

blocks.title: Sample Problem 4.6
blocks.problem: Juglone, is a dye and is produced from the husks of black walnuts. The formula for juglone is C₁₀H₆O₃. a) Calculate the molar mass of juglone. b) Calculate number of moles in 0.87 g of a sample of juglone extracted from black walnut husks.
steps: Mass of 1 mol of C₁₀H₆O₃ = 174 g/mol
b) Moles of juglone = Mass / Molar Mass = 0.87 g / 174 g mol⁻¹

blocks.title: Interesting Information!
blocks.text: Juglone, is a natural herbicide (weed killer). It kills off competitive plants around the black walnut tree but does not affect grass and other noncompetitive plants.

blocks.title: Quick Check 4.2
blocks.text:
a) A copper wire contains 27.10 ×10²⁵ atoms of copper. Calculate the number of moles of copper.
b) Calculate the molecules of 1x10⁻⁶ g of isopentyl acetate, C₇H₁₄O₂ which are released in a typical bee sting. How many atoms of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are present in it?

blocks.title: Interesting Information!
blocks.text: Isopentyl acetate (C₇H₁₄O₂) is the compound responsible for the scent of bananas. Interestingly, bees release about 1 μg (1 × 10⁻⁶ g) of this compound when they sting. The resulting scent attracts other bees to join the attack.
